explanation: The procedure explicitly executes SET NOCOUNT OFF instead of SET NOCOUNT ON, so every statement sends extra DONE_IN_PROC row-count messages to the client.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF is used even though the procedure opens explicit transactions (BEGIN TRANSACTION at lines 182 and 239), so a run-time error can leave a transaction open and partially applied.
SELECT * FROM Sales.Orders returns all 16 columns including nvarchar(MAX) Comments/DeliveryInstructions, wasting I/O and breaking callers when the table schema changes.
SELECT TOP (10) o.OrderID from Sales.Orders has no ORDER BY, so which 10 rows are returned is arbitrary and can change between executions.
DISTINCT on o.OrderID is pointless because OrderID is the primary key of Sales.Orders and is already unique; it only adds a sort/aggregate operator.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders permits dirty reads, missing rows, and duplicate rows from page splits during concurrent modifications.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) wraps the filtered date column, so the optimizer cannot seek a date range; use o.OrderDate >= '20160101' AND o.OrderDate < '20170101' instead.
o.CustomerID is int but @CustomerIdText is nvarchar(20); SQL Server converts the nvarchar side and the comparison can fail at run time on non-numeric input.
The catch-all predicate @CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID prevents index seeks on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID and produces a cached plan that suits neither parameter value.
o.Comments LIKE N'%urgent%' begins with a wildcard, forcing a full scan of an nvarchar(MAX) column with no possible index seek.
NOT IN (SELECT i.CustomerID FROM Sales.Invoices) silently returns zero rows if the subquery ever yields NULL; use NOT EXISTS for reliable semantics.
ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) = 1 wraps the indexed CustomerID column in a function, disabling the index seek on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID.
The customer identifier 1 is embedded directly in the predicate instead of being supplied as a parameter.
o.OrderID + 0 = @OrderID performs arithmetic on the primary key column, preventing a clustered index seek; compare the bare column instead.
o.CustomerID <> 1 is a negative predicate that the optimizer resolves with a scan rather than a seek on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID.
Customer identifier 1 is hard-coded in the inequality instead of parameterized.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate, producing the full product of both tables.
SELECT TOP (1) with no ORDER BY returns an arbitrary order/customer pair from the cross join.
Sales.Orders AS o, Sales.OrderLines AS ol with the join condition in WHERE uses deprecated comma-join syntax that hides join intent and risks accidental cross joins.
SELECT TOP (1) o.OrderID has no ORDER BY, so the returned row is nondeterministic.
The correlated (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE ol.OrderID = o.OrderID) runs once per order row; a GROUP BY join or OUTER APPLY aggregate is far cheaper.
The correlated EXISTS against Sales.OrderLines is evaluated per outer Orders row and could be written as a semi-join over a pre-aggregated set.
The CASE WHEN o.Comments IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END expression is duplicated in the select list and ORDER BY; reference the alias via a CTE/derived table to evaluate it once.
ORDER BY 2 depends on select-list position; reordering or inserting a column silently changes the sort to a different column.
OFFSET/FETCH ordered only by o.OrderDate has no unique tie-breaker, so rows can repeat or be skipped across pages; add o.OrderID to the ORDER BY.
The two branches filter OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2 and are disjoint by construction, so UNION adds a needless distinct/sort operation; use UNION ALL.
Order identifier 1 is hard-coded in the first branch's predicate instead of parameterized.
Order identifier 2 is hard-coded in the second branch's predicate instead of parameterized.
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE ol.OrderID = o.OrderID) > 0 counts every matching line when EXISTS could short-circuit on the first match.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID FROM Sales.Orders scans all rows and silently keeps the last value with no error on multiple rows; use SET with a scoped subquery.
@OrderIds is a table variable populated from Sales.Orders; table variables get fixed low cardinality estimates and no column statistics, leading to poor plans.
INSERT ... SELECT TOP (5) o.OrderID has no ORDER BY, so the five rows loaded into @OrderIds are arbitrary.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates the temp table schema implicitly, inheriting types/nullability from Sales.Orders and preventing explicit indexing or a column contract.
SELECT TOP (5) o.OrderID INTO #ImplicitOrders lacks ORDER BY, so which orders are captured is nondeterministic.
#ImplicitOrders is created but never dropped before the procedure ends, leaving tempdb allocation held for the session's scope.
order_cursor iterates Sales.Orders row by row (DECLARE/OPEN/FETCH NEXT) for work that a single set-based statement could do.
The cursor's SELECT TOP (2) o.OrderID has no ORDER BY, so the cursor iterates an arbitrary pair of rows.
The WHILE @Counter <= 1 loop performs iterative procedural work instead of a single set-based statement.
@Sql is built by concatenating CONVERT(nvarchar(20), @CustomerID) into the query text instead of binding a parameter, defeating plan reuse and inviting injection.
EXEC (@Sql) executes a concatenated string with no parameter list, so each distinct CustomerID produces a separate ad-hoc plan.
The OrderID value is concatenated into the @Sql text rather than passed as a bound parameter.
sys.sp_executesql is called without a parameter definition string, so the embedded literal prevents parameterized plan reuse.
#Scratch is explicitly created but never dropped before the procedure ends.
This CATCH block only SELECTs ERROR_MESSAGE() as a result set; it neither THROWs nor returns a failure status, so callers see success after a failure.
RAISERROR is used for a new error path; use THROW so severity/state and the original error context are preserved.
PRINT output is buffered and not consumable as structured diagnostics; log to a table or use RAISERROR ... WITH NOWAIT if progress messaging is required.
Customer identifier 1 is embedded in the WHERE clause instead of being passed via the existing @CustomerID parameter.
The unlabelled date constant '20160101' is embedded in the filter on o.OrderDate; expose it as a parameter or named constant so the boundary is documented.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') has no style argument, so the result depends on session DATEFORMAT/language and may be 2 January or 1 February.
ON COALESCE(o.CustomerID, 0) = COALESCE(i.CustomerID, 0) wraps both join keys in functions, forcing a scan/hash and eliminating index-based join options.
SELECT TOP (1) o.OrderID from the Orders/Invoices join lacks ORDER BY, so the returned row is arbitrary.
Sales.Orders is joined to itself on OrderID only to return o.OrderID, which is already present in the outer row; the join adds cost with no added data.
SELECT TOP (1) o.OrderID in the self-join has no ORDER BY and yields a nondeterministic row.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts every order by an nvarchar(MAX) LOB column, producing a very wide, memory-hungry sort likely to spill to tempdb.
SUM(ol.Quantity) scans the entire Sales.OrderLines fact table with no WHERE restriction for one scalar value.
HAVING ol.OrderID > 0 is a row-level predicate on the grouping column; moving it to WHERE lets the filter be applied before grouping.
ORDER BY OrderCount is pointless because COUNT(*) without GROUP BY always returns exactly one row.
MERGE against Sales.Orders is subject to documented concurrency/deadlock and correctness bugs; use separate IF EXISTS / UPDATE / INSERT blocks.
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET target.Comments = target.Comments writes the column to its existing value, generating log records and locks with no data change.
UPDATE Sales.Orders SET Comments = Comments assigns the current value, causing logging, locking and trigger firing without changing any data.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE Quantity = -1 targets rows by a non-key business value, so an unexpected data state can remove many more rows than intended.
The magic value -1 for Quantity is embedded in the DELETE predicate rather than being a named parameter or lookup.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' holds a worker thread and any open locks for the duration; use external scheduling instead.
BEGIN TRANSACTION here is not wrapped in BEGIN TRY/BEGIN CATCH, so an error between BEGIN and ROLLBACK can leave the transaction open.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON changes session state and couples the procedure to identity-key management, risking duplicate/seed problems.
EXEC sp_who is called without the sys. schema qualifier, forcing an extra name-resolution lookup and risking resolution to a same-named user object.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 silently truncates every subsequent statement's result and is never restored to 0 before the procedure ends.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (99, @NewCategory) omits the column list, so any change to the temp table definition silently misaligns the values.
Category identifier 99 is hard-coded in the VALUES clause instead of being supplied as a parameter.
CustomerName LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' starts with a wildcard, so the unique index UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName cannot be seeked and a full scan results.
@sql is assembled by concatenating @CustomerName into the LIKE pattern instead of passing it as a bound parameter to sp_executesql.
The caller-supplied @CustomerName is concatenated straight into the executable string; a value containing a quote can terminate the literal and inject arbitrary T-SQL.
sp_executesql is invoked with only the statement text and no @params/argument list, so the embedded value prevents plan reuse.
sp_executesql is called without the sys. schema qualifier.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers has no WHERE clause, so every row in the temp table has CustomerCategoryID overwritten.
CustomerCategoryID is set to the magic value 1 rather than a parameter or looked-up category key.
WHERE o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' filters the outer-joined Sales.Orders rows, discarding the NULL-extended rows and silently turning the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
The unexplained date constant '2016-01-01' is embedded in the predicate on o.OrderDate instead of being a documented parameter.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL never evaluates to true under ANSI_NULLS ON, so the query always returns zero rows; use IS NULL.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) is a scalar UDF invoked per row of Sales.Customers, forcing row-by-row evaluation and blocking parallelism.
This CATCH follows BEGIN TRANSACTION/DELETE but never issues ROLLBACK TRANSACTION, so a failed transaction stays open and holds locks.
The CATCH block only SELECTs ERROR_MESSAGE() and neither rethrows with THROW nor returns a failure code, hiding the failure from the caller.
WITH (INDEX = 1) hard-codes an index by ordinal on Sales.Customers; the plan breaks or degrades if indexes are rebuilt, renumbered, or dropped.
Three levels of nested derived tables (t1/t2/t3) wrap a single scan of Sales.Customers; flatten it or refactor to a CTE for readability.
CustomerName LIKE '%A%' begins with a wildcard, forcing a full index/table scan of Sales.Customers.
SELECT * FROM dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti(@CustomerName) exposes every column the function returns, so callers break whenever the function's shape changes.
dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti is a multi-statement table-valued function, which the optimizer treats as a black box with a fixed row estimate; rewrite it as an inline TVF.
